rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
How will you carry out the following conversions : (Any two)
(i) Propanal to Propane
(ii) Ethanal to But-2-enal
(iii) Ethanoic acid to ethanamide
rows.solution:
(i) PROPANAL TO PROPANE — the carbonyl group must be reduced all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), which neither hydride nor catalytic hydrogenation will do.

WOLFF-KISHNER REDUCTION does it in two stages: hydrazine condenses with the carbonyl to give the hydrazone, and heating that with a strong base expels nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}N{-}NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid does the same job in acidic conditions.

(ii) ETHANAL TO BUT-2-ENAL — count the carbons: TWO in, FOUR out, so two molecules must be joined. This is the ALDOL CONDENSATION:
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The enolate of one molecule attacks the carbonyl carbon of the other, and the aldol so formed loses water on warming because the resulting double bond is CONJUGATED with the carbonyl.

(iii) ETHANOIC ACID TO ETHANAMIDE — ammonia gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on heating:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COONH_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.stem:
In the given reaction
\(\mathrm{N_2\,(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2\,(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3\,(g)}\)
the rate of formation of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is \(3{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-4}\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\).
Calculate the
(i) rate of reaction, and
(ii) rate of disappearance of \(\mathrm{H_2\,(g)}\).
rows.solution:
(i) The RATE OF REACTION is one number describing the whole process, obtained by dividing each species' own rate by its coefficient:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2}]}{\Delta t} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{H_2}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NH_3}]}{\Delta t}\)

Substituting the rate of formation of ammonia:
\(\text{Rate} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(\text{Rate} = 1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

(ii) Hydrogen has a coefficient of 3, so it disappears at THREE TIMES the rate of reaction:
\(-\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{H_2}]}{\Delta t} = 3 \times 1{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(= 5{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

A quicker route goes straight between the two species: the equation shows 3 hydrogen consumed for every 2 ammonia formed, so hydrogen disappears at \(\frac{3}{2}\) times the rate ammonia appears — \(1{\cdot}5 \times 3{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-4}\), the same answer. Note that the rate of REACTION is neither of these; it is the number both are derived from.

rows.stem:
(i) State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
(ii) Calculate the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)) of \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) if \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}\) of \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) are 48 S \(\mathrm{cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\) and 400 S \(\mathrm{cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\) respectively.
rows.solution:
(i) KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW OF INDEPENDENT MIGRATION OF IONS states that the LIMITING molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the SUM of the individual contributions of its cation and its anion, each counted as often as the formula unit provides it:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \nu_+\lambda_+^{\circ} + \nu_-\lambda_-^{\circ}\)

At infinite dilution the ions are so far apart that each moves entirely INDEPENDENTLY of the other, which is what makes the simple sum valid.

Its practical value is for WEAK electrolytes, whose \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) cannot be found by extrapolating a graph.

(ii) The degree of dissociation is the ratio of the measured molar conductivity to the limiting value:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{48}{400}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}12\), that is 12% dissociated

The ratio must lie between 0 and 1, which is the check. A value of 0.12 is what one expects of a weak acid, only a small fraction of it being ionised at an ordinary concentration.

rows.stem:
Write the hybridisation and magnetic character of the following complexes :
(i) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\)
[Atomic number : Ni = 28, Co = 27, Fe = 26]
rows.solution:
(i) \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\). Nickel is 28, and four chlorides give \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so nickel is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\).

CHLORIDE is a WEAK field ligand and does not force pairing, so TWO electrons remain unpaired and no \(3d\) orbital is freed. Bonding uses the \(4s\) and three \(4p\): hybridisation \(sp^3\), shape TETRAHEDRAL, and the complex is PARAMAGNETIC, \(\mu = 2{\cdot}83\) B.M.

(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\). Cobalt is 27; the ammines are neutral, so cobalt is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\).

AMMONIA is a STRONG field ligand and pairs those six electrons into the lower three orbitals as \(t_{2g}^6\), freeing TWO inner \(3d\) orbitals. With the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) these give \(d^2sp^3\), shape OCTAHEDRAL, and with every electron paired the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

(iii) \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\). Iron is 26; six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\).

FLUORIDE is a WEAK field ligand, so all five \(3d\) orbitals stay singly occupied and NONE is available. Bonding must reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set: hybridisation \(sp^3d^2\), shape OCTAHEDRAL, and the complex is PARAMAGNETIC with five unpaired electrons, \(\mu = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(i) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)Cl]Cl_2}\)
(ii) What is the difference between an Ambidentate ligand and a Bidentate ligand ?
(iii) Out of \(\mathrm{[Fe(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\), which complex is more stable and why ?
rows.solution:
(i) Fix the oxidation state first. The four ammines and the aqua ligand are neutral, the chlorido ligand gives \(-1\), and two chlorides sit outside — so cobalt must be \(+3\).

Ligands are named in ALPHABETICAL order regardless of charge, and the counter ion is named last:
TETRAAMMINEAQUACHLORIDOCOBALT(III) CHLORIDE

(ii) An AMBIDENTATE ligand has TWO DIFFERENT donor atoms and can bind through EITHER of them — but only ONE AT A TIME, so it remains monodentate. The nitrite ion binding through nitrogen or through oxygen is the standard case, and the two arrangements are LINKAGE ISOMERS.

A BIDENTATE ligand binds through TWO donor atoms SIMULTANEOUSLY, closing a CHELATE RING that includes the metal. Ethylenediamine and the oxalate ion are the standard cases.

So the difference is not how many donor atoms exist but how many are USED at once — a choice of one, against a commitment of two.

(iii) \(\mathrm{[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\) is the more stable, because of the CHELATE EFFECT.

The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE, so three of them close THREE five-membered rings around the iron. Ammonia is monodentate and closes none.

Two reasons make a chelate more stable: once one donor atom has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily, whereas a separate ligand would have to arrive from solution; and releasing the ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one.

rows.stem:
Calculate the emf of the following cell :
\(\mathrm{Zn\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\,(0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel (0{\cdot}001\ \mathrm{M})\ \mathrm{Ag^{+}} \mid \mathrm{Ag\,(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -\,0{\cdot}76\) V and
\(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Ag^{+}/Ag}} = +\,0{\cdot}80\) V
[\(\log 2 = 0{\cdot}3010\), \(\log 3 = 0{\cdot}4771\), \(\log 10 = 1\)]
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: zinc is on the LEFT and so is the anode, oxidised; silver ions are reduced at the right.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}80 - (-0{\cdot}76) = 1{\cdot}56\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing the electrons gives \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\), so \(n = 2\). Solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}56 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}01}{(0{\cdot}001)^2} = 1{\cdot}56 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{10^{-2}}{10^{-6}}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}56 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log 10^{4} = 1{\cdot}56 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 4\)
\(= 1{\cdot}56 - 0{\cdot}118\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 1{\cdot}442\ \mathrm{V}\)

The SQUARED term is where marks are lost: \((0{\cdot}001)^2\) is \(10^{-6}\), not \(10^{-3}\), so the quotient is \(10^4\) rather than 10. The silver ion's coefficient of 2 carries through as an exponent.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the major products in the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow[273-283\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{HNO_3 + H_2SO_4}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}COONa} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CaO}}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NH_2OH}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — All three reactants are printed as DRAWN STRUCTURES, not formulas. (i) a benzene ring (hexagon with an inner circle) bearing CHO, over an arrow labelled HNO3 + H2SO4 above and 273 - 283 K below. (ii) a plain SATURATED hexagon bearing COONa, plus NaOH, over an arrow labelled CaO above and delta below. (iii) CH3 - C = O drawn two-dimensionally with H on a vertical bond below the carbonyl carbon, over an arrow labelled NH2OH. The linear LaTeX in the stem is a faithful reading of each drawing and each is corroborated by the marking scheme's answer (m-nitrobenzaldehyde / cyclohexane / ethanal oxime), but it is not what the page looks like, so the real crop should be attached. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
(i) The \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group is electron WITHDRAWING, and so DEACTIVATING and META DIRECTING. Nitration at low temperature therefore puts the nitro group at the meta position:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} \xrightarrow[273-283\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{HNO_3}/\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{m\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)

The product is 3-NITROBENZALDEHYDE. The low temperature prevents further nitration and keeps the aldehyde group from being oxidised.

(ii) Sodium salt of a carboxylic acid heated with soda lime — sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide — undergoes DECARBOXYLATION, losing carbon dioxide and giving the hydrocarbon with one carbon fewer:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}COONa} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{C_6H_{12}} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)

The product is CYCLOHEXANE. The calcium oxide is there to keep the sodium hydroxide dry and to stop it attacking the glass.

(iii) Hydroxylamine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{H_2NOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}N{-}OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is ETHANAL OXIME, also called acetaldoxime.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Oxidation of propanal is easier than propanone. Why ?
(ii) How can you distinguish between Acetophenone and Benzophenone ?
(iii) Draw the structure of the following derivative :
2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazone of Propanone
rows.solution:
(i) Because oxidising an aldehyde breaks a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond, whereas oxidising a ketone would have to break a \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond.

Propanal's carbonyl carbon carries a HYDROGEN. Oxidation simply replaces it by a hydroxyl, and the \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond is comparatively weak, so even a mild oxidising agent such as Tollens' or Fehling's reagent does the job.

Propanone's carbonyl carbon carries no hydrogen — it is flanked by two carbons — so oxidation must CLEAVE the carbon skeleton itself. That needs a powerful oxidising agent and drastic conditions, and it gives a mixture of shorter acids.

(ii) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide, ACETOPHENONE gives a YELLOW PRECIPITATE of iodoform, because it carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group; BENZOPHENONE has two phenyl groups on its carbonyl and no methyl, so it gives nothing.

(iii) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group of propanone, losing water:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C}{=}\mathrm{N}{-}\mathrm{NH}{-}\mathrm{C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}\)

The ring carries its two nitro groups at positions 2 and 4, counting from the carbon bearing the nitrogen. Such derivatives are orange-red crystalline solids with sharp melting points, which is how carbonyl compounds were identified before spectroscopy.

rows.stem:
A first order reduction takes 30 minutes for 75% decomposition. Calculate \(t_{1/2}\).
Given : [\(\log 2 = 0{\cdot}3\), \(\log 3 = 0{\cdot}48\), \(\log 4 = 0{\cdot}6\), \(\log 5 = 0{\cdot}7\)]
rows.solution:
The reaction is FIRST ORDER, and 75% decomposition leaves 25% — so taking the initial amount as 100, the amount left is 25:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{30}\log\dfrac{100}{25}\)

Using \(\log 4 = 0{\cdot}6\):
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 0{\cdot}6}{30} = 0{\cdot}046\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

Then the half-life:
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{0{\cdot}046}\)

\(t_{1/2} = 15\ \mathrm{min}\)

The answer can be seen at a glance, and it is worth doing so as a check. Falling to 25% is falling by HALF, and then by half again — exactly TWO half-lives. Thirty minutes for two half-lives means fifteen minutes for one, without any logarithms at all.

rows.stem: Write three differences between Lyophobic sol and Lyophilic sol.
rows.solution:
Three differences between a lyophobic and a lyophilic sol.

AFFINITY FOR THE MEDIUM. A LYOPHOBIC sol is "solvent repelling" — its particles have little attraction for the dispersion medium. A LYOPHILIC sol is "solvent loving", its particles strongly attracted to the medium and surrounded by a protective solvent layer.

REVERSIBILITY. A lyophobic sol is IRREVERSIBLE: once coagulated it cannot be re-formed simply by adding the medium back. A lyophilic sol is REVERSIBLE, re-forming on mixing.

STABILITY. A lyophobic sol is UNSTABLE, held together only by the charge on its particles, and is EASILY COAGULATED by a small amount of electrolyte. A lyophilic sol is STABLE, protected by both charge and solvation, and is DIFFICULT to coagulate.

A fourth difference follows from these: a lyophobic sol needs SPECIAL METHODS of preparation, such as Bredig's arc or peptisation, while a lyophilic sol forms on simple mixing.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the dispersed phase and dispersion medium of 'milk'.
(ii) What is the cause of Brownian movement in colloidal particles ?
(iii) Why does physisorption decrease with increase in temperature ?
rows.solution:
(i) Milk is an EMULSION: the DISPERSED PHASE is a LIQUID — droplets of fat and oil — and the DISPERSION MEDIUM is also a LIQUID, water.

An emulsion of this kind, oil dispersed in water, is stabilised by an emulsifying agent; in milk that role is played by the protein casein.

(ii) BROWNIAN MOVEMENT is caused by the UNBALANCED BOMBARDMENT of the colloidal particles by the molecules of the dispersion medium.

A colloidal particle is struck from all sides at once, but at any instant the blows do not cancel exactly, so the particle is pushed first one way and then another in a ceaseless zig-zag.

The movement is important beyond its appearance: it opposes the force of gravity and so keeps the particles from settling, which is one of the two things that make a sol stable — the other being the charge on the particles.

(iii) Because PHYSISORPTION IS EXOTHERMIC.

Adsorption of this kind releases heat — the adsorbate molecules give up freedom of movement and settle onto the surface. By LE CHATELIER'S PRINCIPLE, an exothermic process is driven BACKWARDS by raising the temperature.

The molecular picture agrees: the forces holding the adsorbate are only weak van der Waals attractions, and at a higher temperature the molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape them.

CHEMISORPTION behaves differently at first, increasing with temperature because the chemical bond needs activation energy to form, and only then decreasing.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
| \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}}\) | Cr | Mn | Fe | Co | Ni | Cu | Zn |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|  | \(-\,0{\cdot}91\) | \(-\,1{\cdot}18\) | \(-\,0{\cdot}44\) | \(-\,0{\cdot}28\) | \(-\,0{\cdot}25\) | \(+\,0{\cdot}34\) | \(-\,0{\cdot}76\) |

From the given \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}\) values of the first row transition elements, answer the following questions :
(i) Why is \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/Mn}}\) value highly negative as compared to other elements ?
(ii) What is the reason for the irregularity in the above \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}\) values ?
(iii) Why is \(\mathrm{E}^{\ominus}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}\) value exceptionally positive ?
rows.solution:
(i) Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) has the exceptionally stable HALF-FILLED \(3d^5\) configuration.

Manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\), so losing the two \(4s\) electrons gives an ion with every \(3d\) orbital singly occupied and all five spins parallel — an arrangement of unusual stability, its electrons spread as widely as possible and its exchange energy at a maximum.

The metal therefore gives up those two electrons very readily, and a metal easily oxidised has a highly NEGATIVE reduction potential. At \(-1{\cdot}18\) V manganese is the most negative in the row.

(ii) Because the quantities that determine \(E^{\circ}\) do not vary regularly across the series.

Three steps decide the value — ATOMISATION of the metal, IONISATION to the \(+2\) ion, and HYDRATION of that ion — and the potential reflects their SUM. The sum of the first two ionisation enthalpies varies irregularly, and the sublimation enthalpies of manganese and vanadium are much lower than their neighbours'.

No single trend therefore runs through the row; each element's value is the net result of three quantities pulling in different directions.

(iii) Because copper has a HIGH enthalpy of atomisation and a LOW hydration enthalpy.

The energy recovered on hydrating \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is NOT enough to pay for pulling the atom out of the metal and removing two electrons from it. The books do not balance, so the process is unfavourable and \(E^{\circ}\) comes out POSITIVE at \(+0{\cdot}34\) V — the only such value in the row.

The practical consequence is that copper does not displace hydrogen from acids, and so does not dissolve in hydrochloric or dilute sulphuric acid.

rows.stem:
Write the equation involved in the following reactions :
(i) Rosenmund reduction
(ii) Etard reaction
(iii) Stephen reaction
rows.solution:
(i) ROSENMUND REDUCTION converts an acyl chloride to an ALDEHYDE by hydrogenation over palladium supported on barium sulphate:
\(\mathrm{R{-}COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd}/\mathrm{BaSO_4}} \mathrm{R{-}CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The catalyst is deliberately POISONED, with sulphur or quinoline and by the inert support, so that it is not active enough to reduce the aldehyde further to the alcohol.

(ii) ETARD REACTION oxidises the methyl side chain of toluene to an aldehyde, by way of a brown chromium complex that is then hydrolysed:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}/\mathrm{CS_2}} \text{brown complex} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)

Trapping the product as an inert complex is what STOPS the oxidation at the aldehyde; permanganate or dichromate would carry it through to benzoic acid.

(iii) STEPHEN REACTION reduces a nitrile to an aldehyde with tin(II) chloride and hydrochloric acid, through an imine that is hydrolysed:
\(\mathrm{R{-}CN} + \mathrm{SnCl_2} + \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}CH{=}NH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{R{-}CHO} + \mathrm{NH_3}\)

All three reactions make an ALDEHYDE from something one stage more oxidised or from a different functional group, and all three succeed by stopping the reduction or oxidation at the right point.

rows.stem:
(i) Which acid of each pair would you expect to be stronger ? Give reason.
(I) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) or \(\mathrm{F-CH_2-COOH}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\)
(ii) Distinguish between Pentan-2-one and Pentan-3-one.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In sub-part (i) pair (II) the first compound is printed as a DRAWN benzene ring bearing OH, not as a formula. Transcribed as its formula, which the marking scheme corroborates ('acetate ion is more resonance stabilised than phenoxide ion'), but the crop should be attached so the page is reproduced. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) FLUOROACETIC ACID is the stronger.

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the anion. Fluorine is strongly electronegative and WITHDRAWS electron density through the \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect, spreading the carboxylate's negative charge and stabilising it. The methyl group of acetic acid does the opposite, RELEASING density and intensifying the charge. The \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) values are 2.59 against 4.76.

(I I) ETHANOIC ACID is the stronger — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 4.76 against phenol's 10.0.

Both anions are stabilised by resonance, but not equally. In the CARBOXYLATE ion the charge is shared between TWO EQUIVALENT OXYGEN atoms, both electronegative and both well suited to carry it. In the PHENOXIDE ion the charge is delocalised onto RING CARBONS, which are far less electronegative and hold it less comfortably — and the two resonance forms are not equivalent.

(ii) Use the IODOFORM TEST. Warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide, PENTAN-2-ONE gives a YELLOW PRECIPITATE of iodoform, because its carbonyl carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) group; PENTAN-3-ONE has an ethyl group on each side of its carbonyl and gives no precipitate.

The test responds only to a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group, or to an alcohol that oxidises to one, which is exactly the structural difference between the two ketones.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Transition metals and their compounds show catalytic activities.
(ii) Zn, Cd and Hg are non-transition elements.
(iii) Zr and Hf are of almost identical atomic radii.
rows.solution:
(i) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form INTERMEDIATE compounds with the reactants.

A catalyst works by offering a path of lower activation energy, and a transition metal does this by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another — changing oxidation state as it goes, then returning to its original state so that it is not consumed. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process cycles between \(+5\) and \(+4\) in just this way.

Finely divided transition metals also provide a large SURFACE on which reactant molecules are adsorbed and held close together with their bonds weakened, as iron does in the Haber process.

(ii) Because their d subshells are COMPLETELY FILLED in both the atom and the ion.

A transition element is defined as one with a PARTLY FILLED d subshell in the neutral atom or in at least one of its stable ions. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are \(d^{10}\) as atoms AND \(d^{10}\) as their \(+2\) ions, so neither condition is met.

Everything that follows from a partly filled d subshell is therefore absent: their compounds are white and diamagnetic, they show only the \(+2\) state, they are poor catalysts, and their melting points are unusually low.

(iii) Because of the LANTHANOID CONTRACTION.

Hafnium lies a whole period below zirconium and should be substantially larger, yet both have radii of about 160 pm. The reason is the fourteen lanthanoids that intervene: across that series each added electron enters an inner \(4f\) orbital, which shields poorly, so the rising nuclear charge pulls the outer shells inwards and cancels the increase expected from the extra period.

The two elements consequently behave so alike that they occur together in nature and are notoriously difficult to separate.

rows.stem: Why does aniline not give Friedel-Crafts reaction ?
rows.context: Amines constitute an important class of organic compounds derived by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms of ammonia molecule by alkyl/aryl groups. Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Reactions of amines are governed by availability of the unshared pair of electrons on nitrogen. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Reactivity of aromatic amines can be controlled by acylation process.
rows.solution:
Because the amino group reacts with the CATALYST.

A Friedel-Crafts reaction needs a LEWIS ACID, anhydrous aluminium chloride, to generate the attacking electrophile. Aniline's nitrogen carries a LONE PAIR, which makes it a Lewis BASE — so the two combine at once, forming a salt:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{AlCl_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_2 \cdot \overset{-}{Al}Cl_3}\)

Two things then go wrong together. The catalyst is used up and cannot generate the electrophile; and the nitrogen now carries a POSITIVE CHARGE, which withdraws electron density powerfully and DEACTIVATES the ring, so it will not accept an electrophile even if one is formed.

The same reasoning explains why nitrobenzene is used as a SOLVENT for Friedel-Crafts reactions while aniline cannot even be a substrate.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of their \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\)
rows.context: Amines constitute an important class of organic compounds derived by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms of ammonia molecule by alkyl/aryl groups. Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Reactions of amines are governed by availability of the unshared pair of electrons on nitrogen. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Reactivity of aromatic amines can be controlled by acylation process.
rows.solution:
Increasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)

Read the scale first. A HIGHER \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a WEAKER base, so this order runs from the strongest base to the weakest.

ETHYLAMINE is strongest: its ethyl group releases electron density to the nitrogen, and its cation still has two hydrogens for hydrogen bonding to water. \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) 3.29.

TRIMETHYLAMINE has three electron-releasing groups but a cation with only ONE hydrogen to hydrogen bond, and its nitrogen is crowded, so it falls behind. \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) 4.22.

AMMONIA has no alkyl group at all to help it. \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) 4.75.

ANILINE is much the weakest, and for a different reason altogether: its lone pair is DELOCALISED into the benzene ring and is simply not available to accept a proton. \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) 9.38 — about five orders of magnitude below the others.

rows.stem: How can you distinguish between \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\) and \(\mathrm{(CH_3CH_2)_2NH}\) by Hinsberg test ?
rows.context: Amines constitute an important class of organic compounds derived by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms of ammonia molecule by alkyl/aryl groups. Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Reactions of amines are governed by availability of the unshared pair of electrons on nitrogen. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Reactivity of aromatic amines can be controlled by acylation process.
rows.solution:
Both amines react with BENZENESULPHONYL CHLORIDE, but the products behave differently towards ALKALI, and that is the test.

ETHANAMINE, being PRIMARY, gives a sulphonamide that still carries a hydrogen on its nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2NH{-}C_2H_5} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

That hydrogen is made ACIDIC by the two strongly electron-withdrawing sulphonyl oxygens, so the product DISSOLVES in sodium hydroxide, forming a soluble salt.

DIETHYLAMINE, being SECONDARY, gives a sulphonamide with NO hydrogen left on the nitrogen:
\((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2N(C_2H_5)_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

With nothing acidic to lose, this product is INSOLUBLE in alkali and remains as a precipitate.

So: soluble in alkali means primary, insoluble means secondary. A TERTIARY amine completes the test by not reacting at all, having no \(\mathrm{N-H}\) to substitute.

rows.stem:
Write the structures of A and B in the following reactions :
(I) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn + HCl}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2\ water}} \mathrm{B}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CONH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2 / alc.\ KOH}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Pyridine}]{\mathrm{CH_3COCl}} \mathrm{B}\)

rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — In sub-item (I) the starting material is printed as a DRAWN benzene ring bearing NO2, not as a formula. Transcribed as its formula, corroborated by the marking scheme (A is aniline), but the crop should be attached. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(I) Tin with hydrochloric acid supplies nascent hydrogen, which reduces the nitro group all the way to an amino group:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Bromine in AQUEOUS solution then brominates at all three activated positions at once, the amino group being so strongly ortho, para directing:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{2,4,6\text{-}tribromoaniline}\), which separates as a white precipitate

Stopping at one bromine would require the amino group to be acetylated first.

(I I) Bromine with alcoholic potassium hydroxide is the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION, giving a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethanamine

Ethanoyl chloride then ACYLATES the amine, pyridine being present to absorb the hydrogen chloride and drive the reaction:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CONHC_2H_5}\), N-ethylethanamide

Counting carbons confirms the first step: the amide had three, the amine has two.

rows.stem:
How will you convert the following :
(I) Benzoic acid to aniline
(II) Aniline to p-bromoaniline
rows.context: Amines constitute an important class of organic compounds derived by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms of ammonia molecule by alkyl/aryl groups. Amines are usually formed from nitro compounds, halides, amides, etc. They exhibit hydrogen bonding which influences their physical properties. Alkyl amines are found to be stronger bases than ammonia. In aromatic amines, electron releasing and withdrawing groups, respectively increase and decrease their basic character. Reactions of amines are governed by availability of the unshared pair of electrons on nitrogen. Influence of the number of hydrogen atoms at nitrogen atom on the type of reactions and nature of products is responsible for identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Reactivity of aromatic amines can be controlled by acylation process.
rows.solution:
(I) BENZOIC ACID TO ANILINE, in two steps. Count the carbons — SEVEN in, SIX out — and that loss is the signature of the Hofmann degradation.

Ammonia gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on heating to give the amide; bromine with alkali then degrades it:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)

(I I) ANILINE TO p-BROMOANILINE, in three steps — and the first is PROTECTION.

Bromine water alone would give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, the amino group being far too activating. Acetylating it first MODERATES that activation, so only one bromine goes on and it goes para:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{CH_3COOH}} \mathrm{p\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NHCOCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{p\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\)

Substitution goes PARA rather than ortho because the bulky acetyl group blocks the positions beside it.
